q1.saying: Most commenters call the two-axis framework a workable starting point but not a complete risk determination, asking FDA to account for reversibility, error detectability, time to harm, traceability, autonomy or clinical agency, and patient vulnerability. Many add that human oversight and downstream safeguards should lower risk only with proof they work; several say "incorrect output" omits harms of omission.

q2.saying: Commenters accept directiveness as a continuum and say it should be judged by what an output functionally does—specificity, personalization, urgency, imperative force, omitted alternatives, confidence presentation—not by interface labels or disclaimers. Many ask that it be measured across multi-turn conversational trajectories, and several want anchored rubrics, worked examples, or decision trees for predictability.

q3.saying: Most commenters accept that patient-facing delivery bears on risk but ask FDA not to treat it as automatically higher risk, tying risk instead to clinical consequence, the user's realistic verification path, and enforceable safeguards. They reject disclaimers as mitigation and would credit only tested features: traceable sourcing, calibrated uncertainty, escalation triggers, and comprehension testing in the actual user population.

q4.saying: Most commenters accept that specialist-versus-generalist use bears on risk but reject professional title as the test, urging risk turn on the gap between a function's knowledge domain and the intended user's ability to independently review outputs, validated through error-detection and escalation testing with the least specialized intended user. Cara AI adds a supervised non-clinical worker tier.

q5.saying: Nearly all commenters said the whole conversation or session, not the individual turn, should be the unit of risk assessment, and asked FDA to require adversarial multi-turn trajectory testing (escalation, user pressure, long context, session boundaries).

q6.saying: Most commenters ask FDA to require under- and over-escalation to be reported and gated as separate error classes, not blended into one accuracy or utility score, with sponsors prespecifying context- and capacity-justified asymmetric acceptance criteria (for example minimum sensitivity plus maximum over-escalation rate) that FDA reviews.

q7.saying: Most commenters accept benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation, but attach conditions: assess the final configured device as deployed rather than the underlying foundation model, bind results to an identified configuration, and avoid treating benchmark scores as a surrogate for real clinical performance in higher-risk uses. Several ask FDA to publish how evidence scales with risk.

q8.saying: Most commenters accept scaling premarket evidence to a function's two-axis risk position, but say the framework is unusable until CDRH publishes an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping specifying minimum benchmarking, confirmation tier, third-party involvement and postmarket monitoring; Walnut Hill Medical also wants tiers tied to 510(k)/De Novo/PMA. Several ask to add dimensions such as autonomy and irreversibility.

q9.saying: Most commenters call FDA's benchmarking structure a sound starting point but incomplete, and ask for added elements: adversarial input and cybersecurity testing, human factors, citation and provenance fidelity, multi-turn and edge-of-scope behavior, and external-dependency or degraded-mode performance. Many also object to aggregate or pooled scores, asking for subgroup- and failure-mode-level reporting with separate acceptance criteria for safety-critical failures.

q10.saying: Most commenters say benchmark scores alone cannot establish real-world safety: sponsors should document per-benchmark construct validity tied to intended use, run contamination checks, use sequestered or independently held test sets, and pair benchmarking with clinical confirmation. Sponsor-developed benchmarks are accepted for novel uses, but only with locked thresholds, escrow, or independent adjudication.

q11.saying: Most commenters accept a graduated ladder of clinical confirmation and agree prospective studies need not always be required, but ask FDA to specify how the tier is chosen rather than leaving it to sponsor justification. Common additions: shadow deployment for intermediate risk, characterization of the anticipated real-world input distribution, subgroup and setting reporting, and evaluation of the deployed human-AI team.

q12.saying: Most commenters told FDA to keep synthetic and real-world results separate, and to pool benchmarking with clinical confirmation only if sampling frames are shown exchangeable, with confirmation governing acceptance. They also asked for disaggregated subgroup, scenario and failure-mode reporting instead of single pooled scores, prespecified estimands and precision, and repeated-run variance reporting to handle nondeterministic outputs.

q13.saying: Commenters accept synthetic data only as a supplement — for rare events, adversarial and stress testing, controlled perturbations, and privacy-limited coverage — and not for establishing performance rates, subgroup claims, or benefit-risk conclusions. Most ask FDA to guard against correlated blind spots through generator lineage disclosure and separation, independent or multiple generators, real-world holdouts, and separate real/synthetic reporting.

q14.saying: Commenters ask that comparators be anchored to the device's labeled intended user and the care patients would otherwise receive, with acceptance criteria prespecified from the consequence of an incorrect output. Several reject the "median clinician in practice" bar; clinician panels are validated, blinded adjudication instruments with reported inter-rater reliability, and team performance is primary where labeling requires human review.

q16.saying: Most commenters back a limited third-party role in the tasks where independence is the point—custody of sequestered test sets, benchmark administration, adversarial testing, and clinical adjudication—conditioned on published qualification and conflict-of-interest criteria, multiple accredited providers (often modeled on ASCA/MDDT), and retained sponsor accountability and FDA decision authority. Several note third-party assessment capacity does not yet exist at scale.

q17.saying: Nearly all commenters accept extending the competency-based approach to multimodal, world-model and other architectures, but ask that evaluation target the final configured device's behavior and function rather than its technical design, adding failure modes such as cross-modal consistency, error propagation and agentic authority. Two note benchmarks are thinner here and want clinical confirmation weighted more heavily.

q18.saying: Most commenters accept trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring only under stated conditions: prespecified, enforceable monitoring plans with triggers and thresholds, demonstrated detection speed and coverage, reversible harm, and rollback authority. Many would bar the trade for high-consequence, autonomous, or poorly observable functions. Several question whether monitoring reliably detects novel or unreported failures at all.

q19.saying: Most commenters accept periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and degradation monitoring as complementary but too narrow, urging monitoring of overrides, near misses, subgroup and workflow effects, human-AI team performance, and clinical outcomes. Many ask that reassessment be event-triggered (model, prompt, retrieval, population, or safety-signal changes) alongside a calendar floor, and that version and configuration records be reconstructable.

q20.saying: Commenters accept machine-based supervisory agents as an aid to postmarket monitoring only if the supervisor is validated and independently evaluated—measured detection sensitivity and false-flag rates, version control, audit logs, and re-evaluation over time. The most repeated condition is independence from the monitored device to avoid correlated failure when both share a foundation model, with human adjudication retained for final judgments.

q21.saying: Nearly all commenters accept outside contributions to postmarket monitoring only if roles are split by distinct function, with manufacturers keeping the monitoring program, complaint handling, aggregation, and corrective action. Many ask FDA to specify what manufacturers must supply institutions—version identifiers, logs, notice of model changes—and to name omitted actors such as clinical engineering staff, payers, and patients.

q22.saying: Most commenters propose tiered change control keyed to clinical or behavioral impact, not code magnitude: no re-testing where outputs cannot change, quality-system-managed re-benchmarking against a locked baseline suite, and premarket review for model-family or provider swaps, scope expansion, and agentic action changes.

q24.saying: Commenters overwhelmingly ask FDA to spell out concrete dependency controls: pinning to a version-identified model endpoint, contractual advance change notice and deprecation windows, technical detection through fingerprints, canary and shadow testing, regression re-benchmarking, quarantine and rollback, with the manufacturer accountable for device behavior when upstream models change. Several would tier such changes within a PCCP.

q25.saying: Nearly all commenters accept the master file concept but say voluntary disclosure alone won't close gaps, asking FDA to specify minimum, versioned content—training-data cutoff, model identity and version lineage, known failure modes, subgroup evaluations, change and deprecation notification—keeping the deployed device the unit of evaluation, with sponsors holding contractual information rights. Supernova Technologies questions self-filed disclosures entirely.

q26.saying: Nearly all commenters say agentic devices need evaluation beyond output quality: acceptance criteria applied to complete action trajectories rather than per-step accuracy, enumerated action inventories classified by reversibility, least-privilege tool permissions, confirmation before irreversible actions, audit logs allowing full reconstruction, rollback and safe-state reversion, and prompt-injection testing, with criteria tightening as autonomy rises and human review declines.
